title: August 20 — Listening Section 2
transcript:
PART 2 - The Royal Nature Park

NARRATOR: Section 2. You will hear a podcast about a famous park in Canada. First, you have some time to look at Questions 11 to 14. Now listen carefully and answer Questions 11 to 14.

GUIDE: Good afternoon and welcome to this podcast on the Royal Nature Park. It's a historical park in Canada that was home to First Nations people and early settlers many years ago.

GUIDE: First Nations groups settled in this area around the lake over six hundred years ago, and the discovery of corn residue at the lowest level of the lake led scientists to believe that [[Q11|corn was once cultivated in the area]] by the First Nations people.

GUIDE: This lake, now in the centre of the park, has varying depths and temperatures. Parts of the lake are so deep that there is virtually no oxygen and very little sunlight. This means that [[Q12|plants and fish have trouble surviving there]].

GUIDE: The only natural residents of the lake area are large turtles that lie on rocks at the lake edge. Visitors are asked not to disturb them, although it's fine to take photographs.

GUIDE: The park has a replica of a First Nations village from long ago. This includes reconstructed longhouses, where [[Q13|several families lived together]]. We built them using historical pictures and archaeological findings so that they resemble the houses from more than six hundred years ago.

GUIDE: They're called longhouses mainly because of their shape: they're long rather than high. There were benches on both sides of the house which were used as beds. People used animal furs to keep warm at night, and they built fire pits inside for warmth and cooking, especially during the winter.

GUIDE: The houses were home to a number of families. [[Q14|All members of the families helped to build a house and contributed to the daily work, including children]].

NARRATOR: Before you hear the rest of the podcast, you have some time to look at Questions 15 to 20. Now listen and answer Questions 15 to 20.

GUIDE: There are many things to do and see during the year at Royal Nature Park.

GUIDE: During the spring, treat your taste buds to an event called Sweet Water Season. At this festival, visitors can see how the early settlers tapped maple trees and boiled the sap to [[Q15|make a traditional sweet food]]. Samples are available for those who wish to taste it.

GUIDE: Another favourite event is our Season of the Harvest. During this programme, visitors [[Q16|pick produce]], including apples from the trees and vegetables from the fields. Early settlers relied on these crops for the winter. You can even purchase some of the fresh fruit and vegetables in the gift shop.

GUIDE: Join the Fall into Nature festival for a special [[Q17|live animal show]] involving hawks and other birds of prey. During the display, watch our trained staff work with these creatures. Visitors can even have the thrill of a wild bird landing on their arm.

GUIDE: Our Moccasin Time event is held regularly around the time of the full moon. It starts at eleven p.m. and takes about an hour to cover the park on foot, so you'll need to bring a flashlight. In other words, you'll [[Q18|take a walk at night]]. If you listen carefully, you may hear owls calling to each other as they hunt for food in the dark.

GUIDE: In September, try our Hide and Seek Trail. Take a tour around the lake and you'll see [[Q19|carvings of endangered species]] on fallen trees and logs. These represent wildlife in the area, including bears, birds and reptiles which are rapidly disappearing. See if you can identify the animal in each sculpture.

GUIDE: In the snowy season, join a group and try cross-country skiing on Pine Ridge Way. You'll [[Q20|follow winter trails]] through frosted pine trees and over snow-covered hills. There are many paths, so watch for the arrows on the trees to get back to the visitors' centre and get warm.

NARRATOR: That is the end of Section 2. You now have half a minute to check your answers.
